summary:
North Ossetia–Alania stands under the framework of the Russian Federation, and that framework carries the heaviest anti-trans penalties in Europe. The law signed in 2023 prohibits gender-affirming surgery and legal gender recognition outright; the 2013 'propaganda' statute was expanded in December 2022 to cover all ages and any material that presents gender transition to minors as desirable; and in November 2023 the Russian Supreme Court designated the 'international LGBT public movement' an extremist organisation, which makes participation in LGBT activism a criminal offence nationwide. The US State Department advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries explicit warnings addressed to LGBT travellers.

Foreign visitors fall directly within these statutes. The expanded propaganda law criminalises public expression that could be read as justifying gender transition; foreigners who breach the administrative and criminal codes face arrest, detention of up to 15 days and deportation. The UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) singles out the North Caucasus, which includes North Ossetia–Alania, as the exception to its otherwise non-persecutory reading of Russia: trans people and public LGBT+ advocates there are found likely to face treatment amounting to persecution, with systematic regional campaigns documented between 2017 and 2024, and 2–6 years' imprisonment under the 2023 designation, rising to 6–10 years for organising.

David Isteev of North Caucasus SOS, whose testimony to the Human Rights House Foundation covers this republic, states that there is no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus and that even private existence can trigger violence, detention or forced return to families; he describes the situation as deteriorating year on year. Western travel advisories name North Ossetia–Alania within the wider Caucasus don't-travel area. The practical effect for a trans visitor is that nothing distinguishing about gender presentation, documents or social circles can be assumed to stay private, and that family honour norms and informal security structures can produce detention or removal without any legal process.
tangentialFactors:
The federal enforcement regime the visitor enters has expanded sharply in volume as well as severity. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget in the two years before that report. Human Rights Watch had recorded 101 extremism-related convictions, for alleged participation in the designated 'international LGBT movement' or for displaying its alleged symbols, as of 30 June 2025, with charges brought under both the administrative and the criminal codes; the organisation called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.

The speed of post-designation enforcement was documented by The Guardian on 17 January 2024: within 48 hours of the Supreme Court ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where around 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, and at least two other venues were raided the same night. The Moscow Times (23 June 2025) reported arrests, club raids and extremism charges as the defining features of LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, including a St Petersburg queer woman who described herself as a second-class citizen after the designation. In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Physical coercion is also documented at family level. BBC Russian (27 July 2024) followed 'Ada', a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour, escaping only when police responded to a phone she had found. The federal framework was consolidated further by laws effective 1 July 2023 that effectively reclassify homosexuality as a mental illness.

No Chechnya-scale secret-prison infrastructure and no explicit special-permission entry requirement are documented for North Ossetia itself, which places it below neighbouring Chechnya in the range of formal restrictions while leaving it inside the same federal legal exposure.
localsOnly:
Residents of North Ossetia–Alania live under the same 2023 bans on legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care that apply throughout the Russian Federation, and under the same extremist designation, which has made LGBT activism a criminal act with imprisonment terms of 2–6 years, or 6–10 years where organising is alleged. No route to legal gender change exists anywhere in the republic or the country.

Informal pressure operates alongside the formal law. David Isteev's testimony describes private existence as itself a trigger for violence, detention or forced return to families, driven by family honour norms and informal security structures in the North Caucasus, and describes the conditions as worsening year on year. Systematic regional campaigns were documented between 2017 and 2024.

For legal purposes, the UK Home Office country policy note (June 2025) treats LGBT+ people, including in the North Caucasus, as a particular social group within the meaning of the refugee convention, and finds that trans people and public LGBT+ advocates in this region are likely to face persecution; this sets the assessment standard applied to UK asylum claims from the republic.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Chechnya-scale secret-prison infrastructure and no explicit special-permission entry requirement are documented for North Ossetia–Alania specifically; the absence of such documentation is not evidence that none exists, and the entry requirements recorded in the sources concern federal law only.

No trans-specific case data, conviction counts or detention records for North Ossetia–Alania itself are available in the current sources. The republic-level picture is assembled from regional testimony, the Home Office regional finding and the federal framework, and the numeric index value attached to the republic in the earlier comparison figures (approximately 0.07 below the national figure of 0.12) is not traceable to any source in this inventory and is treated as unresolved.

The Home Office note is an asylum assessment standard, not a statement about what enforcement a visitor will actually encounter on the ground; the sources do not quantify police practice in the republic beyond the defender testimony.
